correctness.rationale: At every subdivision vertex the closed neighborhood has three specified members; hence selected sets cannot omit original vertices from both bipartition classes. When no original is omitted, the selected subdivision vertices are exactly an edge cover. When one side has omissions, every incident subdivision vertex is forced and each remaining original on that side requires an arbitrary nonempty row/column choice. These are disjoint and exhaustive with proved sufficiency. Inclusion-exclusion and the binomial theorem yield the exact polynomial; minimization yields the three-case minimum multiplicity. A direct adjacency-based script exhaustively confirms the full coefficients for seven graphs and exact-arithmetic checks a further 52 parameter pairs. This finite evidence is not used as an infinite proof.

evidence: Magima–Ragukumar, Theorem 2.19, proves the minimum double domination number of the one-step subdivision of a complete bipartite graph is the sum of the smaller part size and twice the larger; the inspected relevant section does not enumerate all sets.
Cabrera-Martínez–Estrada-Moreno derive scalar double domination formulas for rooted products, which are not the one-step subdivision operation considered here.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A known scalar minimum is a necessary consequence of the polynomial, not a dominating theorem for its coefficients. Neither the rooted-product scalar formulas nor the exact-subdivision existence theorem count all at-least-two subsets of the incidence graph.

evidence: The claimed theorem gives a polynomial whose least nonzero coefficient counts surjections for larger smaller-part sizes and has a special \(3^q+2q-2\) value in the two-vertex smaller-part regime.
The October 2024 subdivision article supplies only the least exponent \(p+2q\).
The known edge-cover polynomial accounts for only the family in which every original vertex is selected.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The polynomial implies the scalar minimum, but the converse fails: many different polynomials have the same smallest exponent. The edge-cover polynomial omits disjoint feasible families and thus cannot imply the full result. We exclude both the scalar minimum and the classical edge-cover polynomial from our novelty claim.

evidence: Behtoei–Zarifian arXiv:2408.05783 defines *exact* double domination by equality of every closed-neighborhood count to two; its Theorem 5 characterizes existence for subdivision graphs.
The proposed formula counts every subset with each count at least two; it includes many subsets violating equality.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Exact and at-least-two notions differ by their quantifier. A structure theorem only for exact feasible sets neither characterizes nor counts the larger at-least-two family; it cannot imply the proposed full coefficients without additional information.

evidence: Magima–Ragukumar Table 6 records scalar minimum values, not a double-domination coefficient table.

exact_database_or_table.reasoning: Known edge-cover data alone does not cover all omitted-original configurations; the scalar table does not determine the degree-by-degree counts. Failure to retrieve an equal table is not definitive proof of originality.

value.rationale: A previously published scalar optimum does not distinguish or count the many feasible double-dominating placements. The new result gives the full distribution and the exact multiplicities of all optimal sets on an infinite two-parameter natural family. Its surjection regime and the exceptional smaller-part-size-two regime explain a concrete structural transition; the theorem combines edge-cover constraints and forced rows/columns without asserting that the classical edge-cover polynomial or the known optimum is new.
